entries.defect: The struct name index was keyed only by name, so same-named structs from different modules collided and lookups could return another module's struct.

findings.summary: The plain-struct fallback now looks a struct up by name only, so a same-named struct from another module can be returned.
findings.detail: The old fallback loop required both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new `find_struct_by_name(&name)` ignores the module source. When two modules each define a struct called `Node`, `Item`, etc., a reference to one can be rewritten to the other's TypeId. That gives wrong field layouts and wrong type identity in codegen.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` keeps the last-interned struct for each name, but the replaced linear scans returned the first matching struct in insertion order.
findings.detail: `intern` does `struct_name_index.insert(name.clone(), id)` for every new Struct, and `retain` rebuilds the index the same way. Distinct ResolvedType::Struct values with the same name overwrite each other, so the index points to the most recent one. Such duplicates include identical names in different modules, or a generic template and a later variant with different fields. Every lookup that used to return the first-registered TypeId can now silently return a different, later type.

findings.summary: `known_type_names_cache` is now built only from global maps and drops each module's local type-name maps.
findings.detail: The removed `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also added the current resolver's `struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes` and `generic_newtype_defs`. These per-module maps can contain names that are not keys in the `all_*` maps, such as import aliases or locally registered entries. Such names are no longer recognised as type names, so valid code can be misresolved. The global set also adds generic newtypes from every module, which may wrongly treat identifiers from unrelated modules as types.

grade.reason: Finding 0 says the struct lookup now uses only the name and ignores the module source, so a same-named struct from another module can be returned, which is the known defect.

findings.summary: The plain-struct fallback no longer checks `module_source`, so it can resolve to a same-named struct from another module.
findings.detail: The old fallback matched on both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new code calls `find_struct_by_name(&name)`, which ignores the module. When two modules each define a struct with the same name (e.g. a user `Error` and a stdlib `Error`), the type resolves to whichever struct the index holds. That yields wrong field layouts, a wrong result or codegen errors.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` keeps only the last interned struct for each name, while the replaced lookups returned the first match in table order.
findings.detail: `intern` overwrites the entry whenever another `ResolvedType::Struct` with the same name but different fields or module is interned. `retain` rebuilds the index the same last-wins way. The removed loops over `iter_type_ids()` returned the first matching TypeId. Duplicate names are possible because `Struct` identity includes `module_source` and fields, so the mangled-name lookups can now return a different TypeId than before. This can produce mismatched types after monomorphization.

findings.summary: The global `known_type_names_cache` no longer includes the current module's flat local maps, so names that exist only there, such as aliased imports, are no longer recognized as types.
findings.detail: `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` used to add keys from the per-module `struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes` and `generic_newtype_defs`. These flat maps can contain names under which types are visible in that module, e.g. renamed imports, that are not keys in the `all_*` maps. The precomputed global set only walks the `all_*` maps. Such names are therefore missing from the known type names, and the resolver may misclassify identifiers or miss types.

grade.reason: Finding 0 says find_struct_by_name ignores module_source, so a lookup can return another module's same-named struct, which is the known defect.

findings.summary: The plain-struct fallback now matches on name only, so it no longer checks that the struct's `module_source` matches.
findings.detail: The old fallback required both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. `find_struct_by_name(&name)` returns whatever struct with that name was interned last, from any module. When two modules define a struct with the same name, a type can be rewritten to the other module's struct. That gives wrong field layouts and types in codegen.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` keeps the last interned struct per name, while the old linear scans returned the first one.
findings.detail: `intern` overwrites the index entry whenever another `ResolvedType::Struct` with the same name is interned. That happens for different modules, or for a re-interned struct whose fields or content differ. `retain` also rebuilds the index with last-wins semantics. The replaced loops over `iter_type_ids()` returned the earliest matching TypeId. Mangled-name lookups in monomorphization can therefore resolve to a different, possibly stale or duplicate, TypeId than before.

findings.summary: `known_type_names_cache` no longer includes each module's own local type maps, so names that exist only in a module's local maps are no longer known.
findings.detail: `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also inserted keys from the per-module maps: `struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes` and `generic_newtype_defs`. These maps can hold names that are not keys in the global `all_*` maps, for example imported or aliased names registered under a local name. The new global set leaves them out. Code that checks whether a name is a known type can then misclassify such names, causing spurious resolution errors or wrong path handling.

findings.summary: WASI modules are cached under an interface key derived with `strip_prefix("wasi:").unwrap()`, which can panic or produce keys that do not match the loader's `ModuleSource::Wasi` values.
findings.detail: Every compilation now eagerly parses, binds and desugars every core and WASI module on first use. If any entry in `ALL_WASI_MODULES` lacks the `wasi:` prefix, the process panics. If the stripped path is formatted differently from the `interface` the loader builds from import paths, the cached entries are never hit. Any lex, parse or bind problem in an unused stdlib module also now panics compilations that never import it.

grade.reason: Finding 0 says find_struct_by_name matches on name only and ignores module_source, so it can return a same-named struct from another module, which is the defect the fix addresses.

entries.defect: compile_one used a silent host and threw away the compiler's diagnostics, both through `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` and by silently producing empty output when the dump returned None, so fixture-generation failures were reported with no reason.

findings.summary: Every phase is run with `--skip-empty`, which also swallows compilation failures and deletes the existing golden file instead of failing.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, when `skip_empty` is set, the `Err(e)` branch removes the output file, logs "Skipped", counts it as skipped and continues. The final assertion still passes. The old script ran `exit 1` on any failed dump. Now a compiler regression that breaks a format fixture silently deletes its `.tir`/`.lower`/`.optimize`/`.wir`/`.wat` golden files, and the script reports success.

findings.summary: Concurrency is now one 16 MB-stack compiler thread per CPU, dropping the cap that was added to avoid memory exhaustion and SIGSEGV.
findings.detail: The removed `run_bulk` capped parallelism at half the available CPUs (minimum 2) because each compilation uses a 16 MB stack plus a large heap, and full parallelism caused SIGSEGV under memory pressure. `run_pipeline` spawns `available_parallelism()` workers, each also leaking an 8 MB alternate signal stack. This brings back the crashes the cap was meant to prevent on many-core or memory-constrained machines.

findings.summary: The `tir` phase now emits only the entry-point module, so the format golden `.tir`/`.optimize` files lost all other modules.
findings.detail: The old script used `wado dump --tir`, which dumped every module (allocator, builtin, prelude, wasi, etc.). `compile_one` for `Phase::Tir` breaks after the entry-point module. The regenerated `all.tir.wado`, `mess.optimize.wado` and the others drop large amounts of previously covered output. Changes in non-entry module TIR are no longer caught, and the files no longer match what `wado dump --tir` produces.

findings.summary: Workers and the skip path build output paths differently, so they disagree when the out template contains more than one `{name}`.
findings.detail: Workers build the path from `split("{name}").next()` and `.nth(1)`, which drops everything after a second `{name}`. The skip path uses `Template::output_path` (`split_once`), which keeps the rest of the template. With such a template, skipped files remove a different path than the one compiled files are written to, and written files land at truncated paths.

grade.reason: No finding covers compile_one discarding the silent host's diagnostics or producing empty output without a reason; finding 0 is about --skip-empty swallowing errors, which is a different problem.

findings.summary: Passing `--skip-empty` to every `golden-dump` call makes compilation failures of format fixtures silently delete the golden file instead of failing the script.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, the `Err(e)` branch removes the output file, logs "Skipped" and `continue`s when `skip_empty` is set. That error comes from `compile_one`, i.e. a real compile failure. The old script ran `run_dump`, which did `exit 1` on failure or empty output and only skipped `#![no_prelude]` files explicitly via grep. Now a regression that breaks compilation of a dirty fixture deletes its .tir/.lower/.optimize/.wir/.wat goldens and the script still ends with "Golden format fixtures updated." The final count assertion also passes, because these failures are added to `skip_count`. The breakage is hidden instead of reported.

findings.summary: The parallelism cap that was added to avoid SIGSEGV and memory pressure was dropped; one 16 MB-stack compiler worker is now spawned per CPU.
findings.detail: The removed `run_bulk` capped concurrency at half the available CPUs (minimum 2). Its comments said this kept peak memory predictable and avoided SIGSEGV under memory pressure. `run_pipeline` sets `num_workers = available_parallelism()`. Each worker has a 16 MB stack, an 8 MB leaked alt stack and a full compiler heap. On machines with many cores, or right after heavy builds, this brings back the out-of-memory crashes the earlier code was written to prevent.

grade.reason: No finding covers compile_one throwing away the silent host's diagnostics (via `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` and empty output when the dump returns None); finding 0 is about the script's `--skip-empty` flag hiding errors, and finding 1 is about worker parallelism.

findings.summary: If enough compiler worker threads panic, the pipeline hangs forever instead of reporting an error.
findings.detail: The main thread keeps its own `Arc` holding `read_rx` for the whole run, so the read channel never disconnects. When every worker thread has died from a compiler panic, nothing drains the bounded `sync_channel`, and the reader thread blocks forever in `read_tx.send`. All `write_tx` senders are dropped, so the writer loop ends normally. Then `reader.join()` blocks indefinitely and the workers are never joined. This happens as soon as the number of panicking fixtures reaches `num_workers` while items remain. The old `run_bulk` turned a panicked compiler thread into an error message.

findings.summary: Passing `--skip-empty` also hides real compilation failures: golden outputs are silently deleted and the script still succeeds.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, `skip_empty` applies to the `Err(e)` branch as well as to empty output. If a format fixture stops compiling, its `.tir`/`.lower`/`.optimize`/`.wir`/`.wat` golden file is removed. The run only prints `Skipped ...`, counts it as skipped and exits 0, so the final count assertion still passes. The old script exited with an error when a dump failed. A compiler regression can now delete golden files without anyone noticing.

findings.summary: Files marked `#![no_prelude]` are no longer excluded from phase-output generation.
findings.detail: The script used to skip compiler phase outputs for any fixture starting with `#![no_prelude]`. The new comment claims `--skip-empty` covers this, but the tir-lowered, WIR and WAT phases produce non-empty output, or a compile error, for such files. They will either gain new golden files that were never generated before, or be silently skipped because of a compile failure. The previous intent is not preserved.

findings.summary: Workers build the output path differently from `Template`, so templates with more than one `{name}` give inconsistent paths.
findings.detail: Workers compute the output path from `out_template.split("{name}").next()` and `.nth(1)`. This drops everything after a second `{name}`. The skip path and `Template` use `split_once`, which keeps the full suffix. When a template contains `{name}` more than once, compiled outputs are written to a truncated or wrong path, while skipped files remove a different path.

grade.reason: None of the findings says that `compile_one` throws away the silent host's buffered diagnostics, either through `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` or by returning empty output when a dump field is None. Finding 2 concerns `--skip-empty` swallowing errors in the script, which is a different root cause.

entries.defect: The .tagpr config put keys outside a [tagpr] section, where tagpr silently ignores them, and used `command` (which runs before the version bump) instead of `postVersionCommand`, so Cargo.lock was never synced and `cargo --locked` CI broke.

findings.summary: tagpr runs with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, so the release tag it pushes will never trigger release.yml's `on: push: tags` workflow.
findings.detail: GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events created with the repository's GITHUB_TOKEN, apart from workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch. `Songmu/tagpr@v1` is invoked here without a PAT or GitHub App token, so it uses GITHUB_TOKEN. When the Release PR is merged, tagpr pushes `v<next>`, but release.yml (triggered on `push: tags: v*`) never runs. No binaries or GitHub Release are produced unless someone dispatches release.yml manually, which breaks step 4 of the pipeline described in `.tagpr`. For the same reason, the Release PRs tagpr opens or updates will not trigger CI. The fix is either to pass a PAT/App token to tagpr, or to call the release workflow from tagpr.yml when tagpr's `tag` output is set.

grade.reason: The only finding concerns GITHUB_TOKEN not triggering downstream workflows, not the misplaced .tagpr keys or the use of `command` instead of `postVersionCommand` for syncing Cargo.lock.

findings.summary: tagpr pushes the release tag with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, so the tag push never triggers release.yml and no release is published.
findings.detail: `Songmu/tagpr@v1` runs here without a PAT or GitHub App token, so it authenticates with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events created by `GITHUB_TOKEN`, including tag pushes. When the Release PR is merged, tagpr pushes `v<next>`, but release.yml's `on: push: tags: 'v*'` trigger never fires. The flow described in `.tagpr` (step 4) therefore breaks, and every release would need a manual workflow_dispatch. To fix it, either give tagpr a PAT or App token, or call the release jobs from tagpr.yml when tagpr reports it created a tag.

grade.reason: The only finding is about GITHUB_TOKEN failing to trigger release.yml, not about .tagpr keys sitting outside the [tagpr] section or `command` being used instead of `postVersionCommand`, which left Cargo.lock unsynced.

findings.summary: The tagpr step does not set a `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable, so the action cannot authenticate.
findings.detail: Songmu/tagpr reads its credentials from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable and its documented usage sets `env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. As written, the job likely fails on every push to main. No release PR is opened and no tag is ever created.

findings.summary: A tag pushed by tagpr with the default workflow token will not trigger `release.yml`, so tagpr releases never get built.
findings.detail: GitHub suppresses workflow triggers for events created with the repository `GITHUB_TOKEN`. `release.yml` only listens for `push: tags: v*`. A tag pushed by tagpr with the default token will not start it. Step 4 of the documented flow ("release.yml runs on the tag push") silently never happens. Binaries are only published if someone runs workflow_dispatch by hand. Fixing this needs a PAT or GitHub App token, or having tagpr call the release workflow directly.

findings.summary: `replace_workspace_version` rebuilds the file with `str::lines()` and `\n`, so CRLF line endings are rewritten to LF throughout Cargo.toml.
findings.detail: `lines()` strips the `\r` from CRLF line endings and every line is re-emitted with a bare `\n`. On a Windows checkout with autocrlf, running `mise run bump-version` therefore rewrites every line ending in Cargo.toml, not just the version line.

findings.summary: The workflow_dispatch input `tag` is interpolated directly into a bash script, which allows shell injection.
findings.detail: `tag="${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}"` is substituted into the script text before bash runs. A crafted input such as `v1"; curl ... #` executes arbitrary commands in a job that has `contents: write` permission. Only users who can dispatch the workflow can trigger this, but the value should be passed through an env var instead.

grade.reason: None of the findings mention the .tagpr config placing keys outside the [tagpr] section or using `command` instead of `postVersionCommand`, which left Cargo.lock unsynced.

entries.defect: The response body pump awaited `frame_tx.send` with no time bound, so a client that stopped draining but kept its connection open pinned the handler task's fiber stack forever.

findings.summary: A stuck in-flight request now has no wall-clock bound, so it can pin a worker forever and permanently wedge it at recycle time.
findings.detail:
The old per-request `tokio::time::timeout` around `run_concurrent` is gone. `HandlerTask` can block indefinitely in two ways:
- on `frame_tx.send(..).await` when a client stops reading the body;
- on a guest that never finishes its post-`task return` work.

When the worker reaches `recycle_requests`, it stops pulling from `job_rx` and waits for `inflight` to drain, which never happens. Round-robin `Dispatch` keeps routing 1/N of all requests to that worker; they queue until the channel fills and then all get first-byte 504s. A single misbehaving client can therefore permanently disable a worker.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is refreshed only when the dispatch loop turns, so a long-lived but healthy request on an otherwise idle worker traps the whole store.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` is re-armed only after `select(recv, drain)` yields. Suppose one request streams a body or waits on slow I/O for longer than `timeout_secs + 5` seconds and no other job arrives. The deadline then passes while the loop sits parked. The next time that request's guest code runs, the epoch check fires `Trap::Interrupt` even though the guest never ran away. The store dies, and every in-flight request on that worker is lost.

findings.summary: In-flight concurrency per worker is unbounded, so the pooling allocator's stack pool can be exhausted and trap the store.
findings.detail: The comment says `chan_cap = max_concurrency / workers` keeps in-flight work within the stack pool sized by `total_stacks(max_concurrency)`. However, the worker dequeues every job immediately and pushes it into `inflight` with no limit, so the channel only bounds queued, not executing, work. Under load, the number of concurrently spawned guest tasks (each needing a fiber stack) can exceed the pool. Allocation then fails, `run_concurrent` errors, and the worker drops all its in-flight requests.

findings.summary: The allocator hard-codes the bin table at [8,140) and the first block at byte 152, which assumes `heap_offset` starts at 8 and is only advanced by this function.

grade.reason: Finding 0 explicitly identifies `frame_tx.send(..).await` blocking indefinitely when a client stops reading the body, which pins the worker, matching the known defect.

findings.summary: A single stuck in-flight request can stall a worker for good, and requests routed to it then hang with no timeout.
findings.detail: The old wall-clock `tokio::time::timeout` around `run_concurrent` was removed. A `HandlerTask` blocked on `frame_tx.send().await` (a client that keeps the connection open but stops reading), or one stuck on a host await, now never finishes. Once `handled` reaches `recycle_requests`, the worker enters drain mode and stops reading `job_rx` until `inflight` is empty, which never happens. `Dispatch::submit` keeps round-robining jobs to that worker until its channel fills. After that, `self.txs[idx].send(job).await` blocks indefinitely. The first-byte timeout only starts after `submit` returns, so those clients hang forever instead of getting a 504. A runaway guest pinning the worker thread causes the same queue-up, because the 35s epoch trap covers only pure-wasm execution.

findings.summary: In-flight requests per worker are unbounded, so `--max-concurrency` does not cap fiber stacks and the stack pool can be exhausted.
findings.detail: The worker loop pulls every job off `job_rx` as soon as it arrives and `accessor.spawn`s it into `inflight`, with no limit on `inflight.len()`. The channel capacity (`max_concurrency / workers`) only bounds queued jobs, not running ones. Each running guest task needs an async fiber stack, but the pooling allocator is sized with `total_stacks(max_concurrency)`, and each store's own `run_concurrent` / instantiation also needs stacks. Under more than about `max_concurrency` concurrent requests (for example slow streaming responses), stack allocation fails. That turns into a store error that kills every in-flight request on the worker and forces a rebuild.

findings.summary: A free with `oldsize == 0` and a non-null pointer used to be a no-op but now dereferences `ptr - 8` as a boundary tag.
findings.detail: The old allocator returned early when `oldsize == 0`. Callers that free zero-length buffers with a non-heap sentinel pointer (for example the canonical-ABI convention of using the alignment as the pointer for empty lists, or static data) relied on that. The new code ignores `oldsize` and reads a header at `oldptr - 8`. For a pointer that `realloc` never returned, this reads arbitrary memory: it may trap via `unreachable` when the low bit is clear, or link a fake block into the free lists and corrupt the heap.

findings.summary: The bin-head table and the first-block/alignment invariants assume `heap_offset` is still exactly 8 when the allocator is first used.
findings.detail: The code only bumps `heap_offset` to 152 when it is below 152. If `heap_offset` already starts higher (static data, or other runtime code that bumped it), several things break. The bin-head table at [8,140) overwrites whatever lives there. The first block lands at an address not congruent to 8 mod 16, so payloads are no longer 16-byte aligned. The hard-coded `block > 152` predecessor check then holds for the very first block, so a free reads a 'footer' from non-heap memory and may coalesce into it, corrupting memory.

grade.reason: Finding 0 explicitly identifies that removing the wall-clock timeout leaves a HandlerTask blocked forever on `frame_tx.send().await` when a client keeps the connection open but stops reading, which is the known defect.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is only refreshed when the dispatch loop turns, so a legitimate long-running request kills the whole worker store.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` is re-armed only when a new job arrives or an in-flight task completes. Consider a request that streams or awaits host I/O for longer than `timeout_secs + 5` while no other traffic hits that worker. When the guest next runs wasm, the epoch is already past the deadline and it traps immediately. `run_concurrent` then errors and the worker drops the store, losing every in-flight request on it. The old code bounded each request separately with a fresh store.

findings.summary: The wall-clock per-request bound was removed, so a stuck request can pin a worker forever and block its recycle and shutdown drain.
findings.detail: The previous `tokio::time::timeout(timeout, run_concurrent(..))` covered host awaits that epoch interruption cannot preempt. Examples are `frame_tx.send().await` against a client that keeps the connection open but stops reading, or a guest that awaits indefinitely after sending the head. The `HandlerTask` now stays in `inflight` indefinitely. When the recycle threshold is reached the worker sets `stopping` and waits for `inflight` to drain, so it never accepts new jobs again. It is effectively dead while still receiving round-robin traffic.

findings.summary: `dispatch.submit(job).await` runs before the first-byte timeout starts, so a request routed to a stalled or full worker hangs with no 504.
findings.detail: `mpsc::Sender::send` waits for capacity on a bounded channel. If the selected worker is stuck (draining for recycle, or saturated), the hyper request blocks in `submit` with no timeout at all. The `tokio::time::sleep(timeout)` race is only set up after the send completes. Round-robin selection keeps sending a share of all requests to that worker, ignoring idle ones.

findings.summary: In-flight requests per worker are unbounded, so concurrency can exceed the pooling allocator's `total_stacks(max_concurrency)` and exhaust the stack pool.
findings.detail: The comment claims the channel capacity (`max_concurrency / workers`) bounds in-flight work. However, the worker loop immediately moves every received job into `inflight` via `accessor.spawn`, freeing channel slots, and has no cap on `inflight.len()`. Under load with more than `max_concurrency` concurrent requests (e.g. slow bodies), more async tasks need fiber stacks than the pool holds. Stack allocation then fails, erroring or trapping the store and taking down all in-flight requests on that worker.

findings.summary: Any trap in one request now destroys the shared store, dropping every concurrent request on that worker.
findings.detail: Previously a trap or timeout affected only the request that caused it, because each request had its own store. Now all requests on a worker share one instance. A guest trap, such as a panic in one handler or the epoch trap, makes `run_concurrent` return `Err`. The worker then discards the store, and the `resp_tx`/`frame_tx` of every other in-flight request is dropped. Those requests get truncated bodies or a 500 instead of their own responses.

findings.summary: The allocator hardcodes 152 as the first block address and uses `heap_offset` unchanged whenever it already exceeds 152, which breaks alignment and previous-block coalescing.
findings.detail: `heap_offset` is only bumped to 152 if it is below 152. If the shared global has already advanced, for example because another path used memory first, the first freelist block starts at an arbitrary address. That address is not guaranteed to be ≡ 8 (mod 16), so payloads lose 16-byte alignment. Worse, the `block > 152` predecessor check then reads `block - 8` as a footer even for the first block. It may interpret foreign memory as a free block and call `fl_unlink` on garbage, corrupting the heap.

grade.reason: Finding 1 explicitly names `frame_tx.send().await` blocking forever against a client that keeps the connection open but stops reading, which pins the worker. That is the same root cause as the known defect.

entries.defect: The dataflow walker treated labeled blocks as straight-line code. It recorded no state at a labeled `break`, so the post-block state ignored early-exit paths that skipped syncs emitted inside the block. Later code then missed a re-read or write-back, and the field update was lost (the indent_level drift).

findings.summary: Labeled `break` never commits `ScalarOnly` candidates, and the post-loop write-back was removed, so a labeled break that leaves the HFS loop loses scalar writes.
findings.detail: `walk_stmt` calls `commit_scalar_for_escape` only for `label.is_none()`. `scalarize_loop` now returns an empty `post_stmts` on the assumption that every exit path has already committed. A `break outer_label` (or a break to a labeled block enclosing the loop) taken while a candidate is `ScalarOnly` exits without ever storing `__hfs_F` into `L.F`. The final field value is silently lost. The old code wrote back before every non-enclosing labeled break and also emitted post-loop write-backs.

findings.summary: Sync emitted while walking a sub-expression is placed before the whole statement, so a re-read needed after a call in the same expression runs before that call.
findings.detail: `walk_expr` pushes re-read and write-back stmts into the statement-level `out` vector, which is inserted before the entire stmt. Take `let x = advance(&mut p) + p.pos;` or `sum = sum + f(&mut b) + b.v;`. The call moves the state to `FieldOnly`, and the later read of `p.pos` makes the walker emit `__hfs_pos = p.pos` into `out`. That re-read executes before `advance` runs, so the read sees the pre-call value. A short-circuit `a(&mut b) && b.v > 0` has the same problem. The module docs claim call-site wrapping, but nothing is wrapped at expression position.

findings.summary: Labeled-block and inline-block breaks are not merged into the post-block state, and removing the `__inline_*` exclusion now exposes this on every inlined early-return.
findings.detail: A `LabeledBlock` (stmt or expr) is walked linearly, and the state after it is just the fall-through state. Consider `blk: { b.v = 1; if c { break blk; } call(&mut b); }` followed by a read of `b.v`. The walker believes the state is `FieldOnly` and re-reads from the field. On the break path the scalar holds 1 and the field is stale, so the write is lost. The opposite mismatch (break while `FieldOnly`, fall-through `ScalarOnly`) reads a stale scalar. Inlined `&mut self` methods use `break __inline_*` for returns, and the previous guard (`collect_locals_accessed_inside_inline_blocks`) that kept such locals from being scalarized was deleted.

findings.summary: Nested-loop exit state is a join with no convergence sync, so a break taken while `FieldOnly` can leave a stale scalar that later code trusts.
findings.detail: `walk_nested_loop` sets the outer state to `pick_join_target_for_candidate([entry, body_exit_pre_sync])` but inserts no sync on the break paths. Consider an inner body `bump(&mut s); if cond { break; } s.pos = s.pos + 1;`. The break is taken while `FieldOnly`, and `commit_scalar_for_escape` does nothing for `FieldOnly`. entries.defect: can_move_past only checked whether the intervening statement clobbers the moved expression's reads, not the reverse; a call-containing field initializer could therefore be relocated past an intervening read of a global it mutates, a miscompile.

findings.summary: A call inside the inner initializer is not treated as reading or writing anything, so two calls can be swapped, or an inner call can be moved past a side-effecting statement.
findings.detail: `Call` only sets `calls = true` and adds no reads. Its `local_reads`, `global_reads`, `heap.reads` and `memory.reads` stay empty, so `is_read_free()` returns true. In `can_move_past`, `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)` therefore returns false even when the intervening statement is itself a call (`self.calls && !other.is_read_free()` fails). Calls never set `may_trap`, so the trap check passes too. As a result, `self_N = struct.new Box { value: f() }; g(); use(self_N.value)` is rewritten to run `g()` before `f()`. That reorders arbitrary user side effects such as printing or mutating globals and the heap. The same hole lets an inner call that reads a global or heap cell move past a `GlobalSet`, `StructSet` or store that it depends on.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` only checks whether the intervening statement clobbers the inner expression, never the reverse, so writes inside the inner initializer get reordered.
findings.detail: The predicate evaluates only `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`. It never checks `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)` and never checks write/write conflicts. Suppose the inner initializer writes a local through a `LocalTee` or a `LocalSet` inside an inlined `Block`, writes a global, the heap or memory, or calls a function. Moving it after an intervening statement that reads or writes the same location changes what that statement observes, or changes the final value. Example: inner `{ x = 2; ... }` with intervening `y = x` (or `x = 1`). After the rewrite, `y` sees the stale `x`, or `x` ends with the wrong value.

findings.summary: The trap-ordering rule ignores intervening statements with observable effects that do not trap, so a trapping inner expression can be moved after output-producing calls or persistent writes.
findings.detail: `can_move_past` rejects reordering only when both sides have `may_trap`. Calls never set `may_trap`, and neither do `GlobalSet` or `MemoryGrow`. Take an inner `StructGet` on null, or a divide by zero, followed by an intervening `println(...)` call whose arguments do not read state the inner expression depends on. Before the rewrite the program traps first. Afterwards it prints and then traps, which changes visible stdout and the host-observable global or memory state. This contradicts the doc comment's claim that the result is the same when only one side traps.

grade.reason: Finding 1 identifies that can_move_past checks only int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr) and never expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr), which is exactly the missing reverse check that the fix adds.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` only checks whether the intervening statement clobbers the moved expression, never the reverse, so a side-effecting initializer can be moved past statements that read what it writes.
findings.detail: The pass explicitly drops the `is_pure_for_elision` requirement, so the inner initializer may contain calls, `StructSet`/`ArraySet`, `GlobalSet`, `LocalSet` in a block, or memory stores. `can_move_past` only evaluates `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)` and never `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)`. Example: `self = struct.new Box { value: block { tmp = 1; ... } }; x = tmp; use(self.value)`. Here `x` originally sees the new `tmp`, but after the rewrite it sees the old value. The same happens with `value: g()` where `g` mutates a heap field and the intervening statement is `x = obj.f`. The result is silent miscompilation.

findings.summary: Two calls can be reordered because `may_clobber` ignores calls when the other side has an empty read set, and calls are not considered to trap.
findings.detail: `may_clobber` returns false for a call when the other expression is read-free. For an initializer like `f(1)` (calls=true, no reads) and an intervening `g(2)` statement, int.may_clobber(expr) is false. The both-trap check does not fire either, because `Call` never sets `may_trap`, so the move is allowed. `self = Box{value: f(1)}; g(2); use(self.value)` becomes `g(2); use(f(1))`. This reorders two arbitrary user calls and changes I/O order, state and which trap fires first.

findings.summary: Calls (and `ArrayClone` with a copy helper) are not marked `may_trap`, which weakens the trap-ordering guard in `can_move_past`.
findings.detail: Callees can trap (unreachable, OOB, etc.), but `Call`/`CallIndirect`/`CallRef` never set `may_trap`. So an initializer containing a call can be moved past an intervening statement that traps, such as a div or `ref.as_non_null`, and vice versa. This changes which trap or side effect is observed first. Trap safety is the property the rule is meant to protect, and it is violated for every call-containing expression.

findings.summary: The moved expression's own control-flow effect is not checked, so an initializer containing a `br`/`return`/`unreachable` can be moved past intervening statements.
findings.detail: `can_move_past` rejects only non-linear intervening statements. An inner initializer whose block may branch out, return or hit `unreachable` (control=NonLocal or Conditional with an escape) originally skipped the following siblings. After the substitution, the intervening statements execute first. Their writes then become visible on paths where they previously never ran.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies the same one-sided may_clobber check in can_move_past, where a side-effecting initializer such as a call gets moved past a statement that reads what it writes.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` only checks whether the intervening statement clobbers the inner expression's reads; it never checks the inner expression's own side effects against the intervening statement, so effectful initializers are reordered unsoundly.
findings.detail:
This pass deliberately does not require the field initializer to be pure, so it may contain calls, local/global sets, or heap/memory writes. The predicate evaluates only `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`. The reverse direction is never checked: `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)` and write/write conflicts are ignored. Examples that are wrongly accepted:
- The inner is a Block that does `t = ...` and the intervening statement reads `t`.
- The inner calls a function that updates global G (or the heap) and the intervening statement reads G or the heap.
- Both write the same local, so the final value flips.
After the rewrite, the intervening statement sees stale state or the wrong value survives.

findings.summary: Two calls can be swapped: an intervening call is allowed whenever the inner expression is read-free, for example `Box{ f() }; g(); use` becomes `g(); use(f())`.
findings.detail: In `may_clobber`, `calls` blocks the move only when `other` has reads. An inner initializer such as a `Call` with constant arguments has an empty read set. An intervening `Call` is `Control::Linear` and does not trap, so `can_move_past` returns true. The two user calls then execute in the opposite order, which can visibly change output (e.g. println order) or program state.

findings.summary: If the inner initializer can trap and the intervening statement has observable side effects but cannot trap, the move makes those side effects happen before a trap that originally preceded them.
findings.detail: Condition 3 only rejects the case where both sides may trap. If the inner traps (null `StructGet`, division by zero) and the intervening statement does a global, heap or memory write, or a call to a host function that does not trap, the original program trapped before that effect. The rewritten program performs the effect first and then traps. Host-visible state such as linear memory, globals or printed output differs.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that can_move_past checks only int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr) and not the reverse, so an inner call that updates a global can be moved past an intervening read of that global, which is exactly the known defect.

entries.defect: inflate_get_gzip_header converted each FNAME/FCOMMENT byte to its own char (Latin-1 style), while gzip_compress_with_header wrote the names' UTF-8 bytes, so non-ASCII names and comments came back as mojibake.

findings.summary: Compressing with a preset dictionary produces a non-standard zlib stream: the dictionary bytes are encoded into the output, and the Adler-32 trailer covers dictionary plus data.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` with `has_dict` deflates `combined` (dict + input) and writes `adler32(combined)` as the trailer, while setting FDICT and the dict id. In real zlib the dictionary only seeds the LZ77 window, so the compressed stream encodes and checksums just the input. A standard inflater given the dictionary will either fail the checksum or emit the dictionary bytes as part of the data. The cross-test `wado_streaming_preset_dict_decompressed_by_zlib_rs` skips decompression with zlib-rs because of this.

findings.summary: `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` never loads the preset dictionary into the inflate window, so it cannot decode genuine FDICT streams from zlib or other implementations.
findings.detail: With FDICT set, the code skips the dict id, inflates with an empty window, then drops the first `dict_len` bytes of the output. A real FDICT stream back-references into the dictionary, so inflating it panics with an invalid distance. If inflation happens to succeed, the code silently removes real data bytes. The dict id is also never compared with `adler32(self.dict)`, so a wrong dictionary is not diagnosed.

findings.summary: RAW_FORMAT streams with a dictionary return the dictionary prepended to the decompressed data.
findings.detail: `compress_raw` with `has_dict` deflates dict + input, so the dictionary bytes become part of the payload. `InflateStream::decompress` for RAW_FORMAT calls `inflate_raw(input)` and ignores the dictionary entirely. A round trip therefore yields dict + data instead of data, and the output is wrong for any standard raw inflater that uses the dictionary.

findings.summary: Lazy matching inserts the current position into the hash chain twice, creating a self-loop `prev[pos] = pos`.
findings.detail: At the top of each iteration `pos` is inserted (`prev[pos%32768]=head[h]; head[h]=pos`). In the branch that emits the previous match, the loop `for i in 0..skip-1` starts at `i = 0` and inserts `pos` again, setting `prev[pos] = head[h] = pos`. Later chain walks that reach `pos` keep revisiting it until `max_chain` is exhausted (up to 4096 at level 9). This wastes time and cuts off the older chain entries, so compression gets worse and slower. The last position of each match (`pos+skip-1`) is also never inserted.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` enforces `max_output` only after decompressing everything, so it does not protect against decompression bombs.
findings.detail: `uncompress2` calls `uncompress(input)` with no limit and checks `result.len() > max_output` afterwards. A small malicious input can still expand to gigabytes and exhaust memory before the check runs, which defeats the purpose of an output size limit.

grade.reason: No finding addresses the decoding of gzip FNAME/FCOMMENT as Latin-1 instead of UTF-8 in bytes_to_string.

findings.summary: Preset-dictionary support is not zlib-compatible: the compressor deflates the dictionary bytes into the stream, and the decompressor inflates without a dictionary window, then drops the first dict.len() bytes.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` compresses `dict ++ input` and sets FDICT. It also computes the Adler-32 trailer over the combined bytes. Any standard zlib inflater given the dictionary will therefore return the dictionary followed by the data. In the other direction, `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` inflates without preloading the dictionary into the window. Real FDICT streams from zlib/zlib-rs that back-reference the dictionary then fail with an invalid distance, or produce wrong output once dict_len bytes are stripped. The DICTID is also never checked against the supplied dictionary.

findings.summary: Lazy matching re-inserts the current position into the hash chain, creating a self-loop `prev[pos] = pos`, and never inserts the last skipped position.
findings.detail: When the deferred match wins, the loop `for i in 0..skip-1` starts at i=0 and inserts `pos` again, although `pos` was already inserted at the top of the iteration. This sets `prev[pos%32768] = head[h] = pos`. Later chain walks that reach `pos` spin on the same candidate until `max_chain` is exhausted, so older candidates are never examined. Position `pos+L-2` is also never hashed. The result is worse compression and far more wasted 258-byte compares at levels 4-9, including the default level.

findings.summary: Gzip file names and comments are corrupted for non-ASCII bytes because `bytes_to_string` turns each byte into its own char.
findings.detail: `gzip_compress_with_header` writes the UTF-8 bytes of the name/comment via `get_byte`. `inflate_get_gzip_header` rebuilds the string with `buf[i] as char`, which treats each byte as a Latin-1 code point and re-encodes it. For example, 'é' (2 bytes) becomes two 2-byte characters, so header round-trips and interop with real gzip files produce wrong names and comments.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` only checks `max_output` after the entire stream has been decompressed, so the limit gives no protection against decompression bombs.
findings.detail: The function calls `uncompress(input)` first, which inflates everything into memory, and only then compares the result length with `max_output`. A small malicious input can exhaust memory or trap before the limit is ever checked, defeating the purpose of the size-limited API.

grade.reason: Finding 2 correctly identifies that bytes_to_string casts each byte to its own char (Latin-1 style) while the compressor writes UTF-8 bytes, which corrupts non-ASCII gzip names and comments.

findings.summary: Preset-dictionary zlib streams are encoded and decoded in a non-standard way, so they do not interoperate with real zlib.
findings.detail:
`DeflateStream::compress_zlib` with a dictionary deflates `dict ++ input`, so the dictionary bytes become part of the compressed stream. It still sets FDICT and writes a DICTID, and the Adler-32 trailer covers `dict ++ input` instead of only the data. A standard zlib `inflate` + `inflateSetDictionary` will output the dictionary followed by the data and then fail the Adler-32 check.

The reverse direction is also broken. `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` never seeds the inflate window with the dictionary. It skips the DICTID without checking it against `self.dict`, inflates the raw data, and then drops the first `dict.len()` bytes. A genuine zlib FDICT stream, whose back-references point into the dictionary, fails with an invalid-distance error. A wrong dictionary of a different length silently returns wrong data, because the checksum is computed over the combined bytes.

findings.summary: In RAW_FORMAT, `DeflateStream` with a preset dictionary emits the dictionary bytes as part of the output.
findings.detail: `compress_raw` deflates `dict ++ input` when `has_dict` is true. Any raw inflater, including Wado's own `inflate_raw` and `InflateStream` in RAW_FORMAT, therefore decodes the dictionary followed by the payload. The result is a corrupted, longer output instead of the original data. A preset dictionary should only prime the LZ77 window, not appear in the stream.

findings.summary: Lazy matching re-inserts the current position into the hash chain, creating a self-loop in `prev[]` that cuts off older match candidates.
findings.detail:
On the path where the previous match is better, the code has already inserted `pos` this iteration (`prev[pos]=head[h]; head[h]=pos`). The skip loop then starts at `i = 0` and inserts `pos` again, so `prev[pos % 32768] = head[h] = pos`. Later chain walks that reach this node keep visiting `pos` until `chain_count` hits `max_chain`, so every older candidate is unreachable.

The loop also stops at `skip - 2`, so the last covered position is never inserted. The output still decodes correctly, but at levels 4-9 compression ratio drops and searches do wasted work.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` only checks `max_output` after decompressing everything, so the limit protects nothing.
findings.detail: `uncompress2` calls `uncompress(input)`, which inflates the entire stream into memory, and only then compares the length against `max_output`. A small malicious input such as a decompression bomb still allocates the full decompressed size, possibly exhausting memory, before the panic. A caller who relies on the size limit to bound memory use is not protected.

grade.reason: None of the findings address the Latin-1 versus UTF-8 decoding of gzip FNAME/FCOMMENT in bytes_to_string; they cover dictionaries, lazy matching, and uncompress2 limits.

entries.defect: write_atomic named its temp file only by process id, so concurrent threads in one process writing the same cache path shared one temp file and could rename it out from under each other, causing failed writes.

findings.summary: A locked generator version is used even when it no longer satisfies the `[build-dependencies]` requirement, so a stale `wado.lock` silently pins the old generator.
findings.detail: `resolve_build_dependencies` and `CliGeneratorProvider::resolve_version` take `locked_versions.get(package)` whenever it is present. They never check it against the manifest's `version` requirement or the lock's `deps-hash`. Example: bump `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.0.9" }` to `^0.1.0` without running `wado update`, and both compile and `wado fetch` keep pulling and running 0.0.9 with no diagnostic. The same applies to `[dependencies]` components via `registry_component_needs`/`locked_registry_versions` in wado-lsp: it trusts any lock entry by id, regardless of the requirement.

findings.summary: The integrity digest recorded in `wado.lock` is never checked when a registry generator (or library component) is pulled or read from the cache.
findings.detail: `wado update` records `integrity` for each `[[build-dependency]]`. However, `resolve_spec`, `fetch_build_dependencies` and `dep_component::pull_component` pull the artifact by tag, never compare it with the locked digest, and write it into the shared `~/wado` cache. Later builds then trust that cached file unconditionally (`is_file()` / `try_read_spec_cache`). A re-tagged or compromised registry artifact, or a tampered cache file, is executed as a build-time generator or composed into the output without detection. This defeats the lock's integrity pinning.

findings.summary: `write_atomic` names its temp file only by process id, so concurrent writers inside one process (parallel async resolutions) share and clobber the same temp file.
findings.detail: The temp path is `component.tmp-<pid>`. Two tasks in the same `wado` process can write the same cache entry at once, for example the generator specs `lib:gale` and `wado-lang:gale`. They have different module keys but resolve to the same coordinate and version, hence the same cache path. Both tasks truncate and write the same temp file concurrently, and one renames it into place while the other is still writing. This can publish a truncated or partial `component.wasm`, which the `is_file()` cache check then trusts permanently. The error is also swallowed by `write_spec_cache`.

findings.summary: An `@version` pin in `module:` overrides the declared `[build-dependencies]` requirement and the lock without any validation.
findings.detail: In `resolve_version` an explicit pin returns immediately. So `module: "wado-lang:gale@0.0.1"` runs 0.0.1 even when the manifest requires `^0.0.9` and the lock pins 0.0.9. There is no diagnostic for the mismatch. In inline mode a pin also silently wins over a conflicting `generator.version`.

findings.summary: `cache_root` only consults `WADO_ROOT` and `HOME`, so on platforms without `HOME` (Windows) every registry dependency and generator fails to resolve.
findings.detail: With neither variable set, `cache_root()` returns `None`. Every registry dependency then lands in `unresolved` with a 'set WADO_ROOT' reason, and `cache::root()` errors. On Windows `HOME` is normally unset (`USERPROFILE` is used), so compile, fetch and LSP resolution of registry deps break there unless the user sets `WADO_ROOT` manually.

grade.reason: Finding 2 identifies the pid-only temp file name in write_atomic, which lets concurrent writers in the same process share and clobber one temp file; this is the same root cause the fix addresses.

findings.summary: A `wado.lock` generator pin is used without checking it against the manifest's version requirement, so a stale lock silently selects a version the manifest no longer allows.
findings.detail: `resolve_version` returns `locked_versions.get(package)` before it looks at `req`. `locked_generator_versions` builds that map from the lock with no `deps-hash` staleness check and no `req.matches()` test. Suppose the user bumps `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1" }` but keeps a lock pinned to 0.0.9: the compile, `check` and `wado fetch` keep pulling 0.0.9 with no diagnostic. The map is also keyed only by coordinate (registry ignored), so a pin recorded for a different registry is applied too.

findings.summary: Registry generator components are pulled and cached by tag only; the lock's recorded `integrity` digest is never verified.
findings.detail: `wado update` records the manifest digest of the `core-kiln-generator` artifact as `integrity`. However, `resolve_spec`, `fetch_build_dependencies` and `try_read_spec_cache` fetch by mutable OCI tag and execute the bytes without comparing them to the locked digest. A re-pushed or tampered tag runs a different generator at build time, silently. This defeats the reproducibility and supply-chain guarantee the lock appears to provide.

findings.summary: A `lib:` nickname spec with no `[build-dependencies]` entry is treated as a literal registry coordinate `lib:<nick>` and fetched from the registry.
findings.detail: In the inline/single-file branch, `package = parts.key`, which can be `lib:gale`. `lib:` is a reserved alias namespace, not a publishable coordinate. When a default registry exists, the provider lists tags and pulls from `<registry>/lib/<nick>/core-kiln-generator`. The user gets a confusing network or 'no published version' failure instead of an error that the nickname is undeclared. The inline path has no `package` field to supply the real coordinate, so the alias can never resolve correctly.

findings.summary: A path build-dependency that declares no `core:kiln/generator` world now produces a wrong error claiming the source is git/workspace.
findings.detail: `rewrite_build_dep_modules` leaves the module as `Spec` when the path dependency has no generator world entry. `resolve_spec` then finds the entry and hits the `let ... Registry ... else` branch. It reports "must resolve to a registry or path [build-dependencies] entry; git and workspace sources are not supported", even though the entry is a path dependency. The previous specific 'declares no [world]."core:kiln/generator" entry' diagnostic is lost.

findings.summary: `fetch_build_dependencies` reports every resolved entry as fetched, so `wado fetch` over-counts.
findings.detail: The function skips already-cached generators but returns `resolved.len()`, while its doc says it returns the number pulled. `wado fetch` adds this to its component count and prints a 'Fetched ...' line for each generator, even when nothing was downloaded.

grade.reason: None of the findings mention write_atomic's temp file being named only by pid, or threads in one process clobbering each other's temp file.

findings.summary: Options field, record and enum names recovered from the component WIT are kept in kebab-case, so multi-word generator options can never be matched by Wado use-site option keys.
findings.detail: WIT record fields and enum cases are kebab-case: a Wado `max_depth` field is lowered to `max-depth`. `record_descriptor` copies `field.name` verbatim into the `OptionsDescriptor`, and enum variants are copied the same way. Inline `options: { max_depth: 1 }` keys are Wado identifiers and cannot contain `-`. Any registry generator with a multi-word option therefore either rejects the supplied key as unknown or reports the required `max-depth` field as missing, because WIT carries no defaults. The canonical options sent to the generator would also use names that do not match the source-path descriptor.

findings.summary: Registry generator components (code executed at build time) are pulled and cached by mutable version tag without verifying the integrity digest pinned in `wado.lock`.
findings.detail: `wado update` records `integrity` (the manifest digest) in `[[build-dependency]]`. `resolve_spec`, `fetch_build_dependencies` and `try_read_spec_cache` only use the version tag: they pull `<repo>/core-kiln-generator:<ver>` and trust whatever bytes come back, and later trust whatever file sits in `~/wado/`. A re-pushed or compromised tag, or a tampered shared cache, silently substitutes the generator that runs during compilation. The lock's integrity pin provides no protection.

findings.summary: The locked generator version is used unconditionally, even when the lock is stale and no longer satisfies the `[build-dependencies]` requirement.
findings.detail: `resolve_build_dependencies` and the provider's `resolve_version` take `locked_versions.get(package)` whenever an entry exists. They never check the version against the manifest `version` requirement or the lock's `deps-hash`. Suppose a user bumps `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1" }` but does not run `wado update`. `wado fetch`, `check` and `compile` keep silently using the old 0.0.x generator, which violates the declared requirement and gives no staleness diagnostic.

findings.summary: In single-file inline mode a `lib:` nickname specifier is used directly as the registry coordinate.
findings.detail: When the key is not in `[build-dependencies]`, `resolve_spec` sets `package = parts.key`. For `module: "lib:gale"` with an inline `registry`/`version`, this lists tags and pulls `lib/gale/core-kiln-generator` from the registry, which is a nonexistent repository. The inline generator form has no `package` field, so `lib:` cannot be resolved. The specifier should instead be rejected with a clear error.

findings.summary: An explicit `@version` pin in a generator specifier is accepted verbatim, without validation and without checking it against the build-dependency requirement or the lock.
findings.detail: `resolve_version` returns `pin` immediately. A range such as `wado-lang:gale@^0.1` becomes a literal OCI tag, causing a confusing fetch failure. An exact pin outside the declared `[build-dependencies]` requirement silently overrides both the requirement and the lock pin, so the build no longer reproduces `wado.lock`.

findings.summary: `cache_root` only consults `WADO_ROOT` and `HOME`, so registry dependencies never resolve on platforms without `HOME` such as Windows.
findings.detail: When neither variable is set, `cache_root()` returns None. Every registry need then errors with `set WADO_ROOT`, and `crate::cache::root()` fails `wado compile`/`fetch` with "cannot locate the home directory". On Windows, `USERPROFILE` is the usual home variable, so registry deps and generators break by default.

entries.defect: When a provider's dependency was dead-code-eliminated and never added to dep_instances, compose_dependency_components bailed with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' instead of skipping the unused provider, so compilation failed.

findings.summary: A provider whose dependency is imported but never called makes composition fail with "no composed dependency imports provider interface".
findings.detail: `resolve_inline_providers` builds a provider for every `use ... with { provider }` directive in every loaded module, whether or not the dependency is used. `dep_instances` holds only assets whose interfaces or world functions appear in the import plan. A dependency that is imported with a provider but never called is therefore never instantiated. The provider loop then finds no importer and runs `anyhow::bail!`. As a result an unused (or not-yet-used) import breaks the build in the composition step instead of compiling or giving a source diagnostic.

findings.summary: `imported_cm_interface_fqs` still lists guest-effect interfaces that a provider satisfies and composes away.
findings.detail: World-function entries are dropped here because `wasm-compose` removes them. A `Component` entry, however, still inserts every `host_leaf_imports_for(fq)`, and that includes the guest-effect FQ (e.g. `test:hlc/highlight`) that a provider now satisfies. The consumer's reported import surface (world checks / embedded WIT) therefore claims a non-WASI import the final composed artifact no longer has. That can wrongly reject the program for a fixed WASI world, or embed an incorrect contract.

findings.summary: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` rejects or registers every non-`#[cm]` interface in the entry module, including effects fully handled inside the library.
findings.detail: The collision check and the registration loop run over all interfaces in the entry module without checking whether the effect actually escapes the library boundary. An effect that is handled internally, or any plain interface whose kebab name equals the package interface (e.g. `Hltest` in package `hltest`), makes `--lib` compilation fail with a spurious "collides" error. Every such interface also gets a minted CM import identity even though it never becomes an import.

findings.summary: Guest effects declared in non-entry modules of a `--lib` package are never registered as CM imports.
findings.detail: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` is passed only the entry module (`entry`). A library whose unhandled effect interface lives in a submodule and escapes through a facade `export fn` gets no registration. It falls back to the unresolved-call ICE this change was meant to remove.

findings.summary: World-level function signatures that use component-defined named types are not rejected and will ICE in codegen.
findings.detail: `emit_world_function` maps each param and result type with an empty interface FQ (`map_type(resolve, p.ty, "")`), and no check rejects named types. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` documents that such signatures are rejected, yet calls `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty type-index maps. Importing a component whose world function takes or returns a record, variant, etc. therefore panics or produces a wrong encoding instead of giving a diagnostic.

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed only by bare name, so same-named functions from different dependencies (or a local function) silently overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` writes `effect_to_func[func_name]` and `world_import_functions`. `register_component_decls` writes `world_import_sources[name]`. Two component dependencies that both export a world function `highlight` overwrite each other's signature and source. Calls from one dependency's binding then fail the source check or bind to the other's signature. Composition would also try to connect both dependencies to the single program import.

findings.summary: The LSP always passes an empty provided-import set to `check_semantics`, so code that relies on `with { provider: ... }` gets a false missing-effect error in the editor.
findings.detail: The batch compiler discharges a reconstructed guest effect (e.g. `Highlight` required by `Hlc::wrap`) when a provider is supplied. The LSP never runs `resolve_inline_providers` and calls `check_semantics(&sem, IndexSet::default())`. A file like `provider_surface.wado`, which compiles and runs, therefore shows `missing effect 'Highlight' required by 'Hlc::wrap'` in the editor. `check_effects_semantic` and `check_default_purity_semantic` also hard-code an empty set.

findings.summary: World-level function imports have their effects cleared unconditionally, ignoring the dependency component's own host-leaf or guest imports.
findings.detail: For a world function the adapter's `effects` are cleared, and `imported_cm_interface_fqs` drops `ImportKind::WorldFunction` entirely. A dependency whose world-level export uses WASI (e.g. stdout) or imports a guest interface is still treated as pure. Effect checking then never requires the capability or a handler or provider. The composed component keeps the dependency's leftover imports, but they are missing from the computed import set and world contract. The result is a missed diagnostic, and an artifact whose declared imports do not match what it actually needs.

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed globally by bare snake-case name, so two dependencies exporting the same function name collide.
findings.detail: `world_import_functions`, `world_import_sources` and `effect_to_func` are all keyed by the bare function name. A second dependency exporting e.g. `highlight` overwrites the first one's source and `CmFunctionInfo`, so calls can route to the wrong dependency. In `compose_dependency_components`, both assets also match `world_func_cm_names` and both get connected to the same program import, which makes `graph.connect` fail with a composition error.

findings.summary: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` mints CM imports for every non-`#[cm]` interface in the entry module and maps every declared method parameter, including any receiver.
findings.detail: Any user `interface` in a `--lib` entry module is registered as a CM import whose CM names come from kebab-cased Wado names. All `method.params` are mapped into CM params without excluding a `self` receiver. If an interface is used as a trait with `&self` methods rather than as an effect, its methods get bogus import signatures that include a self parameter. The lowering could then emit a malformed import or misroute trait calls.

findings.summary: The documented `--implement <fq>` flag is never parsed: `parse_args` hard-codes `lib_interface_export: false`.
findings.detail: `CompileOptions::lib_interface_export` is documented as the CLI's `--implement <fq>`, but `parse_args` always sets it to false and no option sets it. A user cannot build a provider component from the CLI; the build silently produces a plain library whose exports may not be grouped under the interface the consumer imports.

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed only by their bare name, so two component dependencies that export a world function with the same name overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `world_import_functions`, `world_import_sources` and `effect_to_func` are all keyed by `func.name` alone. If two dependencies both export e.g. `highlight`, the second registration replaces the first `CmFunctionInfo` and `ModuleSource`. Calls to the first dependency's function then fail the `world_import_source(name) == Some(&module_source)` check and are never retargeted to an adapter, leaving an unresolved call. At composition, both assets list `highlight` in `component_world_func_names`, so both try to `connect` to the same single program import, which fails.

findings.summary: A provider directive on a dependency the program never calls makes composition bail with "no composed dependency imports provider interface".

Providers from `with { provider: ... }` are always passed through, and the early return is skipped whenever `providers` is non-empty. If the consumer imports `hlc.wasm` with a provider but never calls into it (or the calls are removed), no dependency instance exists. The provider loop then hits `anyhow::bail!`, and an otherwise valid program fails to compile.

Two use decls naming the same component with a provider produce two `ProviderComponent`s with the same `import_fq`. `compose_dependency_components` then connects both provider exports to the same dependency import. A component that exports a world-level function but itself imports e.g. `wasi:filesystem` keeps that import after composition. findings.summary: A world function whose signature uses a component-defined named type is not rejected as documented and instead hits an internal panic.
findings.detail: The doc comment says named types in a world function signature are rejected. Nothing produces such a diagnostic, though. `emit_world_function` maps types with an empty interface fq, and `generate_cm_world_func_imports` calls `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty type-index maps. A record or variant in the signature therefore reaches an unresolved-type lookup or panic (ICE) instead of a user-facing error.
